titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — §112–126: carriage, debt-hostages and deposits (xviii 50 – xxi 24)

draftNote: The § chips number the laws (Harper’s sectioning, still standard); long laws span several tap-units. Readings checked sign-by-sign against Harper’s 1904 edition.

about: Fifteen laws on goods entrusted to other people. The first are the carriage laws: a man away on a journey gives silver, gold and goods to a man to carry, and if the carrier keeps what he was meant to deliver he is convicted and pays five times its value (§112). Then the debt-hostage laws: a creditor who helps himself to grain from a debtor’s bin or storehouse, without the owner’s say, loses his whole loan and returns what he took (§113); one who holds no debt yet seizes a person pays a third of a mina for each (§114); a hostage who dies a natural death in the creditor’s house costs him nothing (§115), but one who dies from beating or neglect costs the creditor his own son, if the hostage was a free man’s son, or a third of a mina and his loan, if a slave (§116). Debt can also put a man’s wife, son and daughter into service for three years, with release in the fourth (§117); a slave handed over can be sold on by the merchant (§118), but the slave-woman who has borne her master children can be redeemed (§119). The last six laws are on deposits: grain stored in another man’s house, lost or taken or denied there, is doubled by the one who took or denied it (§120), and storing grain costs five qa per kor a year (§121); valuables given for safekeeping need witnesses and a contract, and without them there is no claim (§122–123), while a depositary who denies a deposit made before witnesses pays double (§124); a house-owner in whose house a deposit is lost, through a breach or a crossing-over that also took his own goods, must make good what he was careless with and then look to the thief himself (§125); and a false report of loss turns the claim round on the one who made it (§126). Harper’s transliteration is followed with his glossary; where a Sumerogram stands on the plate behind a printed Akkadian word (Á for hire, KI.UD for the storehouse, the fraction one third, the capacity sign SÌLA) the note says how far the identification can be checked, and two readings, ubâršuma and babtašu in §126, are given with their alternative.

sentences.i: If a man is away on a journey and has given silver, gold, stones and his own goods to a man, and had him carry them as a consignment,
sentences.n: The carriage laws begin; this first law is a long “if”. ina ḫarrānim wašib “he is staying on the road” (wašābum, to dwell, stay): the owner is away. Three goods stand side by side, kaspam ḫurāṣam abnam, then u bīš qātīšu: bīšum is Harper’s “property, possessions”, here in the short construct form bīš, and qātīšu is “of his hands” (so spelled in the earlier parts), so “his own goods”. abnum is simply “stone”; beside silver and gold it presumably means precious stones. iddinma is nadānum, “to give”, with -ma “and”. A šubultum (Harper: “goods for transportation”) is a consignment; ušābilšu is the Š-stem of wabālum “to carry”, so “he had (him) carry”. Uncertain: whether -šu is “him” (the carrier) or “it” (the consignment).

The last verb is inaddin, “he shall give”, the present used for the code’s “shall”.

sentences.i: and the merchant passes the slave on and sells the slave for silver, no claim shall be made on the slave.
sentences.n: Here the merchant who holds the slave is free to move him on. ušētiq is etēqum, “to pass”, in the Š-stem (causative), preterite: “he made (him) pass (to another)”; ana kaspim inaddin, “for silver he gives”, is sale. ul ibbaqqar is the N-stem of baqārum (Harper’s BAKARU IV), “he shall not be claimed”: nobody can reclaim the slave from the buyer. Uncertain: whether ušētiq belongs to the merchant’s act of passing on or to the owner’s. Because ušētiq is a preterite, not a permission, the two verbs are read as a further condition (the English present, “passes on and sells”, covers both), with the ruling in ul ibbaqqar; either way the sense is that the merchant may sell him on and the buyer cannot be claimed against.

sentences.i: the owner of the slave-woman shall weigh out the silver the merchant paid, and redeem his slave-woman.
sentences.n: The mother of children is not lost for good: kaspam tamkārum išqulu, “the silver (that) the merchant weighed out” (a ša-less relative clause with the subjunctive -u), is repaid by bēl amtim, “the owner of the slave-woman”, and then amassu ipaddar, “he shall redeem his slave-woman” (padārum, Harper’s “to ransom”). sentences.i: If a man has stored his grain for storage in a man’s house, and an accident has happened in the granary,
sentences.n: The first of the deposit laws, on grain. ŠE-šu is “his grain”, šeʾišu. ana našpakūtim is “for storage” (the abstract in -ūtum, “being stored”, built on našpakum, Harper’s “heap, bin”; compare maṣṣarūtum “safekeeping”). The text has bīt awīlum, with -lum, where the genitive -lim is expected: Harper prints a-wi-lum as it stands. išpukma is šapākum, “to heap up, store”, with -ma. garītum is Harper’s “store-house, granary”. ibbûm (i-ib-bu-u-um) is his “accident”; the grain is damaged or lost by something outside anyone’s fault, and what follows says who bears it. ittabši is the perfect of the N-stem of bašûm, “to be there, come about”: “has happened”. Uncertain: ibbûm and its sense of “accident”, as it occurs only here.

sentences.n: The ruling. maḫar ilim, “before the god”: the proof is made in front of the deity, the same phrase as in §9. ubârma is bârum in the D-stem, “to prove, establish” (Harper: “to declare, itemize”): the owner states and proves the amount of his grain. sentences.i: If a man has stored grain in a man’s house, he shall give, each year, five qa of grain for each kor as the hire of the bin.
sentences.n: The price of storage. išpuk is the plain preterite of šapākum (§120 had išpukma). ina šanat, “in the year” (šanat, a form of šattum), means “each year”. The rate: ana 1 ŠE.GUR.E, “for one kor of grain” (the signs ŠE, GUR and a final E; E is as in GAN.E, the bur, in §44), ḫamšat qa šeʾim, “five qa of grain”. The numeral 5 is five wedges (Harper’s V) and the measure is the sign he reads QA, qa, about a litre; the plate draws it as a diamond with a cross, which I take to be SÌLA. Á našpakim is “the hire of the bin”: Harper’s ID is the ideogram for hire, idum (his glossary lists it among the Sumerian ideograms, with -šu and -ša). On the plate it is one sign, A₂ (Á, “arm; hire”), the same sign that spells it in ittabši and not the river sign A.ENGUR, so “hire” rests on his list and not on a spelled word, and the case ending is not written. Five qa for three hundred: a little under two per cent a year.

sentences.i: If a man’s goods are not lost, but he says that his goods are lost, and has made a claim against the one he holds liable,
sentences.n: The last law of the part: a false report of loss. lā ḫaliqma, “is not lost, and”, then mimmēšu ḫaliq iqtabi, “his goods (are) lost, he said”: ḫaliq is the stative, iqtabi the perfect of qabûm, “to say”. babtum is Harper’s “loss, defects” (written ba-ab-ta-šu), and utebbir (u-te-ib-bi-ir) his “to file a claim for” (abārum, “to accuse”; Harper’s stem II,2, the reflexive of the D-stem, here a preterite). Harper brackets mi-im-[me]-šu: the oblique-looking mimmēšu where a subject is expected is as he prints it. Uncertain: I take babtašu as the person he holds responsible, “his babtum”, which the rest of the law needs (a payment to him in the last line); on Harper’s reading, “he filed a claim for his loss”, the same sentence would stand with babtašu as the loss, but then ana babtišu in the last line is not a payment to anyone. He also brackets ḫa-li-[iq]. Later dictionaries have babtum as a city quarter or ward, which would make “his babtum” the accused man’s quarter; Harper’s “loss, defects” is the base here, and the person held liable is the nearest to both.

sentences.i: since his goods were not lost, the one he accused shall prove it against him before the god, and
sentences.n: kīma mimmûšu lā ḫalqu, “since his goods are not lost” (kīma, “since, when”, with the stative ḫalqu and the subjunctive -u). Then babtašu ina maḫar ilim ubâršuma: ubâršu is bârum, D, “he shall prove”, as in §120, with -šu “him”; babtašu is the subject, set first, and -šu is “him”, the claimant: “his babtum, before the god, shall prove him”, i.e. the accused proves the matter against the man who accused him, here that the goods were never lost. Uncertain: who the subject of ubâršuma is. The other reading takes babtašu as the object, taken up by -šu, with the claimant as the subject; Harper’s own gloss for ubâršu is “to declare, to itemize”. “Prove” stays as the base sense of bârum.

glossary.kaspum: silver — the code’s money, written KÙ.BABBAR “shining precious-metal” · kaspim: mišil mana kaspim “half a mina of silver” · with a spelled vowel after the logogram: KÙ.BABBAR-a-am, -i-im, -u-um: kaspam, kaspim, kaspum (accusative, genitive, nominative); kaspum as the subject; the grain-and-silver pair šeʾam u kaspam “grain and silver”
glossary.kiššātum: service, being held in service for a debt (Harper: kiššatu “service”; a different word from kiššatum “totality” of the prologue): kiššātim (ki-iš-ša-tim, ki-iš-ša-a-tim), ana kiššātim “into service”
glossary.kurrum: the kor, a grain measure (written GUR; Harper: 300 KA): kur šeʾam “a kor of grain” · written GUR.É (the editors’ print GUR-É) as well as GUR: 1 GUR.É, kurrum “a kor” (UNCERTAIN: the .É is not explained here) · written ŠE.GUR.E, with a final E: ana 1 ŠE.GUR.E “for one kor (of grain)”; the .E is not explained here, UNCERTAIN
glossary.kânum-D: D-stem of kânum: to convict, prove against someone (uktīn, ukannūšuma) · uktīn (uk-ti-in, perfect, with the infixed -t-) “he has convicted”; ukannūšuma (u-ka-an-nu-šu-ma, present, plural, with -šu “him” and -ma) “they shall convict him, and”; ukānma (u-ka-an-ma, present, singular) “he shall convict, and”
glossary.kīma: like, as · as, like; with a verb in the subjunctive: kīma ubbalu “as he brings (it)” · according to: kīma ṣimdat šarrim “according to the king’s schedule” · “since, when”, before a stative: kīma mimmûšu lā ḫalqu “since his goods are not lost”
glossary.leqûm: to take: ileqqi “he shall take” · ilqi “he took” (il-qi₂), ilqû (subjunctive, il-qu₂-u₂), ilqēma (il-qi₂-e-ma) “he took, and”, ilteqēma (perfect, il-te-qi₂-ma) “he has taken, and”; ša … ilqû “which he took” · ilqēma (il-qi₂-ma) “he took, and” (preterite ilqe + -ma, here without a spelled e); ilteqe (il-te-qi₂, perfect) “he has taken”; ileqqi (i-li-qi₂, present) “he shall take”; leqîm (li-qi₂-im, infinitive, genitive): ina kaspim leqîm “in the taking of the silver”
glossary.lā: not (in subordinate and nominal contexts) · before a noun in the genitive, “without”: lā kanīkim “without a sealed receipt”; in a šumma-clause, “not”: lā ītamar “he did not see”
glossary.makkūrum: property, assets — written with the Sumerogram Harper reads ŠA.GA (modern NÍG.GA)
glossary.mala: as many as, as much as (introducing a relative clause): mala ina kirîm ibbaššû “as many as are in the orchard”
glossary.manûm: mina — weight of silver, 60 shekels (about 500 g): 1 mana kaspim · spelled in syllables, ma-na, at §59: mišil mana kaspim “half a mina of silver”
glossary.maškanum: storehouse, granary (Harper: “granary, storage-house”): maškanim (ma-aš-ka-nim) “of/in the storehouse”; also written with two Sumerogram signs KI.UD, which Harper’s glossary names KISLAḪ for maškanum; the identification of the pair is checked only on the plate, UNCERTAIN
glossary.maḫar: before, in the presence of: maḫar ilim “before the god”
glossary.maḫāṣum: to strike; of ground, to break up: imaḫḫaṣ “he shall break up” · the noun maḫāṣum “beating, abuse, injury” (Harper), written ma-ḫa-ṣi-im with the sign ZI (value ṣi): maḫāṣim “(through) beating”
glossary.mimmûm: property, belongings: mimmûšu “his property” · mimmâšu (mi-im-ma-šu, accusative) “his goods”; mimmûšu (mi-im-mu-šu) “his goods” as subject; mimmê (mi-im-me-e, oblique): itti mimmê bēl bītim “with the goods of the owner of the house”; mimmēšu (mi-im-me-šu, oblique-looking, bracketed by Harper) “his goods”
glossary.mâtum: to die: imtūt (im-tu-ut, perfect) “he/she has died”, so ina šīmātīša imtūt “she died a natural death”
glossary.mārtum: daughter (written DUMU+ti): mārtišu “his daughter” · mārassu (DUMU.SAL-zu, three signs DUMU + SAL + ZU, ZU for -ssu) “his daughter”
glossary.mārum: son (DUMU) — here: a minor, not yet able to sell · member of a group: mārū ugārim (DUMU A.GÀR{meš}) “the sons of the irrigated land”, the district’s farmers · mār awīlim “a man’s son” (DUMU); mārī (DUMU{meš}) “sons” (oblique plural, which may include daughters, so “children”); māršu (DUMU-šu) “his son”
glossary.nabalkattum: UNCERTAIN: apparently “crossing-over”, a noun from the root BLKT of nabalkutum “to cross over”; nabalkatka “your crossing-over (?)”; the sense is a guess, and the word is broken in places (naba…, …katim) · nabalkattim (na-ba-al-ka-at-tim, split by the stone over two lines) after ina, beside ina pilšim “through a breach”: a second way into a house, read “by crossing-over (the wall)”; Harper’s glossary has “pillage”; the sense stays UNCERTAIN
glossary.nadānum: to give, pay: inaddin, iddinam, iddinušum; nadānim “to give” · iddin “he gave”; ana kaspim nadānum “to sell”: inaddinūma (present, plural) “they shall sell, and …” · iddin, iddinu “he gave” (preterite; the subjunctive -u in a ša- or inūma clause); iddinma “he gave, and”; …in, …din in broken forms; inaddin “he shall give”: ana damqaršu inaddin “he shall give to his merchant” · ittadinma (it-ta-di-in-ma) “he has given, and” (perfect); inaddinu (i-na-ad-di-nu) “(which) he gives” (present, with the subjunctive -u) · ittandin (it-ta-an-di-in, perfect with an extra -n-) “he has handed over”: ana kiššātim ittandin “he handed over into service”; ittadin (it-ta-din) “he has given”, i.e. sold; ana maṣṣarūtim inaddin “he gives for safekeeping”; iddinūšumma “they gave him, and”
glossary.nadānum-N: N-stem of nadānum: to be given: innaddin “it shall be given”, innaddiššumma “it shall be given to him” · innadnušum (preterite, subjunctive -u, dative -šum) “(which) was given to him”
glossary.nakārum: UNCERTAIN: perhaps nakārum “to be hostile, to deny, to dispute”: only the first sign ik survives, which the editor doubts, so the form (ikkir-ma ?) and the sense are a guess; the verb is the editors’ restoration · ittakir (it-ta-ki-ir, perfect) “he denied, disowned (his merchant)”, ittakiršu “he denied him”, ikkiru (ik-ki-ru, preterite with the subjunctive -u) “(because) he denied”: here the forms are spelled out on the stele, so the verb nakārum is sure; Harper’s heading is “to be different, to be hostile, to dispute” · ittakir (it-ta-ki-ir, perfect) “he denied” a deposit: ana gamrim ittakir “he denied it altogether”; ittakiršu (it-ta-ki-ir-šu) “he has denied him”; ittakrūšu (it-ta-ak-ru-šu, perfect, plural, with -šu) “they have denied him”; ikkiru (ik-ki-ru, preterite with the subjunctive -u) “(whatever) he denied”: the verb is spelled out on the stele in these laws, so nakārum “to deny” is sure here
glossary.našpakum: bin, store for grain (Harper: “heap, bin”): našpakam, našpakim (na-aš-pa-kam, na-aš-pa-ki-im; the last syllable of -kam is the sign KAM), ina našpakim “from the bin”
glossary.našpakūtum: storage, being stored: the abstract in -ūtum built on našpakum “bin”: ana našpakūtim (na-aš-pa-ku-tim) “for storage”, as maṣṣarūtum is “safekeeping”
glossary.nebûm: to distrain, seize as a pledge (Harper; later dictionaries write nepûm, with p): ittebi (it-te-bi, perfect) “he has distrained”; ibbima (ib-bi-ma, preterite + -ma) “he distrained, and” (Harper lists ib-bi under this verb); nēbīša (ne-bi-ša) “her distrainer”, the one who holds the hostage (a noun from the verb, with -ša; the exact shape of the noun is UNCERTAIN)
glossary.nibūtum: hostage for debt, a person taken as pledge (Harper: “hostage”; from nebûm; later dictionaries write nipûtum, with p, from nepûm): nibūtum, nibūtim; nibūssu (ni-bu-zu, the sign ZU standing for -ssu, nibūt + -šu) “his hostage”; ana nibūtim “for a hostage”
glossary.padārum: to ransom, redeem (Harper): ipaddar (i-pa-dar, present) “he shall redeem”
glossary.petûm: to open; of land, to bring into cultivation: iptete “he has opened” · preterite ipte, iptēma “he opened”
glossary.pilšum: the breach, the burglar’s hole: ina pani pilšim “in front of the breach”
glossary.qabûm: to speak, say: iqbû, iqtabi, iqabbûma
glossary.qûm: the qa, a capacity measure of about a litre (Harper: QA), written with the sign SÌLA: ḫamšat qa šeʾim “five qa of grain”; the identification of the plate’s sign as SÌLA is the editor’s, UNCERTAIN
glossary.qātum: hand: ina qāt “from the hand of” · qātīšu (qa₂-ti-šu) “of his hands”: bīš qātīšu “his own goods”
glossary.ragāmum: to claim, to call out a claim: irgumu (ir-gu-mu, preterite with the subjunctive -u) “(whatever) he claimed”
glossary.rebûm: fourth: rebûtim šattim “in the fourth year”
glossary.tabālum: to take away, carry off: itabbal · tabal “take!” (imperative) · itbal (it-ba-al, preterite) “he took away”
glossary.tamkārum: merchant (written tam-KAR §32, DAM.GÀR §40): the ransom-fronting, land-buying businessman of the code · written dam-qar, dam-qar-um (the common syllabic spelling of the merchant): damqar, damqarum “the merchant” (nominative), damqaršu “his merchant” · written DAM.GÀR as a Sumerogram (Harper tamkaru [DAM-GAR]; two signs on the plate): tamkārum, tamkāram, tamkārim, tamkāršu
glossary.târum-D: D-stem of târum: to give back: turru “taken away/captured”; utarrūšumma “they shall return (it) to him” · utâr (present) “he shall hand back” · turrim (infinitive, tu-ur-ri-im): ana turrim “for repaying, to give back”; utâr (present) “he shall hand back” · uttēr (ut-te-ir, perfect) “he has given back”: the same verb as utâr
glossary.ulu: or (u-lu, a conjunction, “or … or”): ulu … ulu “either … or”, “or … or”, linking the clauses of a list
glossary.wabālum-Š: Š-stem of wabālum “to carry”: to make carry off, let (water) carry away: uštābil (perfect) “he has let (the water) carry off” · ušābilšu (u-ša-bil-šu, preterite) “he had (him) carry”; šūbulu (šu-bu-lu, Š stative šūbul with the subjunctive -u) “(what) has been sent”, šūbulūma (šu-bu-lu-ma) “has been sent, and”; the stative reading is from the form and the exact sense is UNCERTAIN
glossary.walādum: to bear, give birth to: ūlidušum (ul-du-šum) “(whom) she bore to him” (preterite ūlid, the long ū of a w-initial verb, with the subjunctive -u and the dative -šum; Harper’s spelling is shortened, so the vowels of the form are UNCERTAIN)
glossary.wardum: male slave (ARAD) · warad (ARAD, no ending written) “male slave of …”, wardam (ARAD-am)
glossary.wašābum: to sit: ul uššab “he shall not sit” (the stone writes uš-ta-ab — a carver’s slip Harper flags) · to dwell: wāšbum (participle, contracted) “the dweller, the tenant” (a conjectured reading, aš-bu-u[m]); wa… “dwell-” in broken forms · stative wašbat (wa-aš-ba-at) “she dwells, lives”: ša ina gagîm lā wašbat “who does not live in the cloister” · stative wašib (wa-ši-ib-ma, with -ma) “he is staying”: ina ḫarrānim wašib “he is staying on the road”
glossary.šakānum: to set, place: išakkanūšumma “they shall set for him (a term), and” · išakkanūšum (present, plural, dative -šum) “they shall place (it) for him”, i.e. count it to him · iššakkan (iš-ša-ak-ka-an, N-stem present) “it shall be put”: ul iššakkan “it shall not be put (in the account)”
glossary.šalāmum-D: D-stem of šalāmum “to be whole, sound”: to make good, restore (Harper: “to restore”): ušallamma (u-ša-lam-ma) “he shall make good, and”
glossary.šanûm-Š: UNCERTAIN: šanûm “to repeat, do a second time”, so perhaps “to double”; uštašannâ (uš-ta-ša-an-na-ma, with -ma “and”) is a Š-stem perfect (ušta- is the perfect prefix) and is read as “he shall double (it)”, but the exact stem and the form are not secure; the sense follows the penalty of the law · on the stele (§101): uštašannâma (uš-ta-ša-na-ma, with -ma “and”) “he shall double (it)”, which Harper’s glossary lists as a Š-stem perfect of šanû “to duplicate, to double”; the form is as Harper has it and the exact stem is not secure
glossary.šapākum: to heap up, store (grain): išpuk (iš-pu-uk, preterite) “he has stored”; išpukma (iš-pu-uk-ma) “he stored, and”
glossary.šapākum-N: N-stem of šapākum: to be stored: iššapku (iš-ša-ap-ku) “(which) was stored” (passive with the subjunctive -u)
glossary.šaqālum: to weigh out (silver = to pay): išqulu · išaqqal (present) “he shall weigh out”
glossary.šarrāqānum: thief (Harper): šarrāqānišu (šar-ra-qa₂-ni-šu) “his thief”, the thief in question
glossary.šattum: year: šattam (syllabic, §31) or MU (the year-sign, §30) · šattim (genitive); plural šanātim “years” (ša šanātim “of the years”); MU 4{kam}, said erbe šanātim “four years” · MU 3{kam}, said šalāš šanātim “for three years”; šanat (ša-na-at) “(in) the year”, ina šanat “each year”
glossary.šeʾum: barley, grain (the ŠE sign) · ŠE-am, ŠE-im, ŠE-um, written with the logogram and a spelled vowel; šeʾum as the subject; ŠE-am-ma “grain only” (with the restricting -ma); in broken forms še…
glossary.šeʾûm-Gtn: Gtn-stem (repeated action) of šeʾûm “to seek” (Harper: “to search for”): ištenēʾima (iš-te-ne-i-ma, present, with the infix -ten-) “he shall search about, and”; the stem analysis is from the form, UNCERTAIN
glossary.šubultum: consignment, goods sent for carriage (Harper: “goods for transportation”): šibultim (ši-bu-ul-tim) in bēl šibultim “the owner of the consignment”, ana šibultim “as a consignment”
glossary.šumma: if — the word that opens every law of the code
glossary.šuāti: that, the aforesaid · as the independent pronoun “him”: šuāti u bīšašu “him and his goods”
glossary.šīmtum: fate; one’s natural death: ana šīmtim ittalak “he went to (his) fate” = he died · plural šīmātum “fates”: šīmātīša (ši-ma-ti-ša) “her fates”; ina šīmātīša imtūt “she died in her fates” = she died a natural death
glossary.ḫalāqum: to be lost, vanish: ḫalqu, ḫalqam · iḫtaliq (iḫ-ta-li-iq, perfect) “it has been lost”; ḫaliq (ḫa-li-iq, stative) “(it) is lost”, ḫaliqma “is lost, and”; lā ḫaliqma “is not lost, and”
glossary.ḫalāqum-D: D-stem of ḫalāqum “to be lost, to perish”: to destroy, cause to be lost: uḫalliqu (preterite, with the relative -u) “(the grain) he destroyed”
glossary.ḫarrānum: road; campaign: ḫarrān šarrim “the king’s campaign” (spelled ḫar-ra-an, or carved with the road-sign KASKAL) · journey, the merchant’s trading trip: ana ḫarrānim “on a journey” (the editors print ḫarranim; the spelling ḫar-ra-nim is uncertain here), ina ḫarrānim “on the journey”
glossary.ṣabātum: to seize: iṣṣabat, ṣabtu · stative with the subjunctive -u: adi kirâm ṣabtu “as long as he holds the orchard” (with Harper’s kirûm: “as long as the orchard is held”) · iṣṣabtamma (iṣ-ṣa-ab-tam-ma) “she seized (them), and” (perfect with the ventive -am and -ma): lā iṣṣabtamma “and she did not seize” · iṣbassuma (iṣ-ba-zu-ma, ZU for -ssu) “it seized him, and” (preterite iṣbat + -šu + -ma), of a debt seizing a man
